questions.q: Which command starts an interactive Python session (the REPL) on most systems where Python 3 is installed?
questions.explain: Running python3 (or python / py on Windows) with no file name opens the REPL, where each line you type is executed immediately.

questions.q: You save print("Hello") in hello.py. How do you run it from a terminal in the same folder?
questions.explain: Pass the file path to the interpreter: python3 hello.py. The interpreter reads the file top to bottom and executes it.

questions.q: In the REPL you type 2 + 3 and press Enter. What happens?
options: 5 is displayed, because the REPL prints the value of each expression
Nothing is shown until you call print()
The REPL saves the result to a file
questions.explain: The REPL evaluates each expression and echoes its value. In a script you would need print() to see it.

questions.q: Which statement about Python files is correct?
options: Indentation is part of the syntax, so consistent spaces matter
Every statement must end with a semicolon
Code blocks are wrapped in curly braces
File names must end in .pyc to be runnable
questions.explain: Python uses indentation to define blocks. PEP 8 recommends 4 spaces per level. Semicolons and braces are not needed.

challenge.title: Your first script
challenge.prompt: Write a script that stores your name in a variable and prints a greeting using an f-string.
challenge.explain: An f-string (prefix f) evaluates expressions inside {} and inserts their values into the text.

questions.q: What does type(7 / 2) return?
questions.explain: The / operator always performs true division and returns a float (3.5). Use // for floor division, which returns an int for int operands.

questions.q: What is the value of 17 % 5?
questions.explain: % returns the remainder: 17 = 5 × 3 + 2, so 17 % 5 is 2.

questions.q: What does int("42") + 8 evaluate to?
questions.explain: int("42") converts the string to the integer 42, so the result is 50. Without the conversion, "42" + 8 would raise a TypeError.

questions.q: Which value is falsy in a boolean context?
questions.explain: The number 0, empty strings, empty containers and None are falsy. The string "0" and the list [0] are non-empty, so they are truthy; -1 is a non-zero number, so it is truthy.

challenge.title: Temperature converter
challenge.prompt: Convert 100 degrees Celsius to Fahrenheit (F = C × 9/5 + 32) and print the result with one decimal place.
challenge.starter:
celsius = 100
# compute fahrenheit and print it
challenge.explain: Division makes the result a float; the format spec :.1f prints exactly one decimal place.

questions.explain: range(3) produces 0, 1, 2. The stop value is excluded.

questions.q: When does the else block of a for loop run?
options: When the loop finishes without hitting break
Only when the loop body raises an error
Every time the loop condition is false on an iteration
Never; for loops cannot have else
questions.explain: A loop's else runs after the loop completes normally. If break exits the loop early, the else is skipped. This is handy for search loops.

questions.q: What does continue do inside a loop?
options: Skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next one
Restarts the loop from the first item
Pauses the program until Enter is pressed
questions.explain: continue jumps straight to the next iteration; break exits the loop.

questions.q: Which Python version introduced the match statement (structural pattern matching)?
questions.explain: match/case arrived in Python 3.10 (PEP 634).

challenge.title: FizzBuzz to 15
challenge.prompt: Print the numbers 1 to 15, but print Fizz for multiples of 3, Buzz for multiples of 5 and FizzBuzz for multiples of both, all on one line separated by spaces.
challenge.starter:
results = []
for n in range(1, 16):
    # append the right value
    pass
print(" ".join(results))
challenge.expected: 1 2 Fizz 4 Buzz Fizz 7 8 Fizz Buzz 11 Fizz 13 14 FizzBuzz
challenge.explain: Check the combined case (divisible by 15) first, otherwise the Fizz branch would catch 15 before FizzBuzz.

questions.q: What does a function return if it reaches the end without a return statement?
questions.explain: Every Python function returns a value; without an explicit return it returns None.

questions.q: Inside def total(*args), what is args?
options: A tuple of all positional arguments passed
questions.explain: *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple. **kwargs collects keyword arguments into a dict.

questions.q: Why is def add(item, items=[]) a common bug?
options: The default list is created once and shared across calls
Default values are not allowed for lists
It makes the function run slower
questions.explain: Default values are evaluated once, when the function is defined. Use items=None and create a new list inside the function.

questions.q: Are type hints like def area(r: float) -> float: enforced when the code runs?
options: No, they are documentation for readers and tools like mypy
Yes, Python raises TypeError on mismatches
Only when the file is named with .pyi
questions.explain: The interpreter does not enforce annotations. Type checkers and IDEs use them to catch mistakes before you run the code.

challenge.title: A reusable function
challenge.prompt: Write a function average(numbers) that returns the mean of a list, or 0 for an empty list. Print the results for [4, 8, 6] and [].
challenge.starter:
def average(numbers):
    # return the mean, or 0 for an empty list
    pass

print(average([4, 8, 6]))
print(average([]))
challenge.explain: Guarding the empty case avoids ZeroDivisionError; sum()/len() returns a float.

questions.q: Which built-in type is ordered and immutable?
questions.explain: Tuples keep their order and cannot be changed after creation. Lists are mutable; sets are unordered.

questions.q: What does {1, 2, 2, 3} evaluate to?
questions.explain: Sets store unique items, so the duplicate 2 is dropped.

questions.q: prices = {"tea": 20}. What does prices.get("coffee", 0) return?
questions.explain: dict.get returns the default (here 0) when the key is missing, instead of raising KeyError like prices["coffee"] would.

questions.q: nums = [3, 1, 2]. What is the difference between nums.sort() and sorted(nums)?
options: sort() changes the list in place and returns None; sorted() returns a new list
sorted() changes the list in place
questions.explain: list.sort() sorts in place and returns None; sorted() leaves the original unchanged and returns a new sorted list.

challenge.title: Word counter
challenge.prompt: Count how many times each word appears in the sentence and print the dictionary.
challenge.starter:
sentence = "the cat and the hat"
counts = {}
# fill counts
print(counts)
challenge.explain: dict.get(word, 0) starts each new word at 0. Dictionaries keep insertion order, so words print in the order first seen.

questions.q: What does f"{3.14159:.2f}" produce?
questions.explain: The format spec .2f rounds to two decimal places.

questions.q: What is "Python"[1:4]?
questions.explain: Slicing includes the start index (1, 'y') and excludes the stop index (4), giving 'yth'.

questions.q: Why do strings have methods like .upper() that return a new string?
options: Strings are immutable, so they cannot be changed in place
To save memory by copying less
Because strings are stored as lists
Python requires every method to return a copy
questions.explain: Strings cannot be modified after creation; methods return new strings, so assign the result: s = s.upper().

questions.q: Which string is a raw string that keeps backslashes literally?
questions.explain: The r prefix disables escape sequences, so \n stays as a backslash and n. That's useful for Windows paths and regular expressions.

challenge.title: Receipt line
challenge.prompt: Print an item name left-aligned in 10 characters and its price right-aligned with two decimals in 8 characters.
challenge.starter:
item = "Tea"
price = 20
# print one aligned receipt line
challenge.explain: In a format spec, < aligns left and > aligns right within the given width; .2f adds two decimals.

questions.q: Why is with open("notes.txt") as f: preferred over calling open() and close() yourself?
options: The file is closed automatically, even if an error occurs
It is the only way to open text files
It locks the file for other programs
questions.explain: The with statement uses a context manager that always closes the file when the block ends, including on exceptions.

questions.q: What does mode "a" do when opening a file?
options: Appends to the end, creating the file if needed
questions.explain: "a" adds to the end of an existing file (or creates it). "w" truncates and overwrites.

questions.q: What is the most memory-friendly way to process a large text file line by line?
options: Reading it into a single string first
questions.explain: Iterating over the file object reads one line at a time instead of loading the whole file into memory.

questions.q: Why pass encoding="utf-8" to open()?
options: So the file reads and writes the same way on every operating system
Because Python cannot read text without it
To open the file in binary mode
questions.explain: Without it, the default encoding depends on the platform. Being explicit avoids surprises with non-English characters.

challenge.title: Write and read back
challenge.prompt: Write three lines to tasks.txt, then read the file and print how many lines it has.
challenge.starter:
tasks = ["buy milk", "call mom", "study python"]
# write the tasks, then count the lines
challenge.solution:
tasks = ["buy milk", "call mom", "study python"]
with open("tasks.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for t in tasks:
        f.write(t + "\n")
with open("tasks.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    count = sum(1 for _ in f)
print(f"{count} lines")
challenge.explain: Each write adds a newline, so the file has three lines; iterating the file counts them without loading it all at once.

questions.q: Which exception does int("abc") raise?
questions.explain: The argument has the right type (a string) but an invalid value for conversion, so Python raises ValueError.

questions.q: When does the finally block run?
options: Always, whether or not an exception occurred
Only if there is no except block
questions.explain: finally runs in every case, which makes it the place for cleanup such as closing resources.

questions.q: Why should you avoid a bare except: clause?
options: It also catches errors you did not expect, hiding real bugs
It makes the program run slower
questions.explain: A bare except catches everything (even KeyboardInterrupt). Catch the specific exceptions you can handle.

questions.q: In try / except / else, when does else run?
options: When the try block raised no exception
questions.explain: else holds code that should run only if try succeeded, keeping the try block small and focused.

challenge.title: Safe number input
challenge.prompt: Write a function to_number(text) that returns the integer value, or None if the text is not a valid number. Print the results for "42" and "forty".
challenge.starter:
def to_number(text):
    # return int(text), or None on failure
    pass

print(to_number("42"))
print(to_number("forty"))
challenge.explain: Catching only ValueError handles bad input while letting unexpected errors surface.

questions.q: What does python3 -m venv .venv do?
options: Creates an isolated virtual environment in the .venv folder
questions.explain: venv creates a self-contained environment so each project can have its own package versions.

questions.q: Which file conventionally lists a project's pip dependencies?
questions.explain: requirements.txt lists packages (often with versions) and is installed with pip install -r requirements.txt.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the if __name__ == "__main__": guard?
options: Run code only when the file is executed directly, not when imported
Mark the file as a package
Required by Python in every file
questions.explain: When a module is imported, __name__ is its module name; when run directly it is "__main__". The guard keeps script-only code from running on import.

questions.q: from math import sqrt lets you call which?
questions.explain: from module import name brings the name directly into your namespace, so you call sqrt(16).

challenge.title: Use the standard library
challenge.prompt: Use the statistics module to print the mean and median of the scores.
challenge.starter:
import statistics
scores = [70, 85, 90, 65, 85]
# print mean and median
challenge.explain: The standard library ships ready-made tools; statistics.mean and statistics.median avoid writing the maths yourself.
